newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S. AFRICAN AUDITOR CLEARS OIL FUND OF MALPRACTICE.
newsitem.headline: S. AFRICAN AUDITOR CLEARS OIL FUND OF MALPRACTICE.

text.p: South Africa's auditor general on Monday cleared the Central Energy Fund (CEF) and its general manager of any error or malpractice concerning an alleged 170 million rand loss from the country's strategic oil stock.
"This amount does not represent a loss or theft of oil or a transfer of oil to any other person. It is simply an accounting entry," Deputy Auditor General Bertie Loots told reporters.

The auditor general, parliament's watchdog on public spending, engaged auditors Price Waterhouse Meyer Nel to examine the CEF's accounts after Mineral and Energy Affairs Minister Penuel Maduna publicly accused the auditor's office earlier this year of "some nimble footwork" to cover the alleged loss of 170 million rand.
"They will have to come up and say how, short of a big fire, they lost stock to the tune of 170 million rand," Maduna said.
Maduna subsequently suspended CEF general manager Kobus van Zyl on full pay pending the outcome of an investigation he ordered by an independent Cape Town-based auditor.
The CEF was set up under apartheid to manage South Africa's oil purchases and stocks in the face of international sanctions imposed in 1977 and lifted in 1994.
Maduna was out of the country on Monday. A spokesman said the ministry would comment on Tuesday on the auditor general's report and its implications for Van Zyl's future.

Loots said the 170 million rand debit in the CEF's accounts for 1993 reflected an accounting adjustment to allow the government to shift some of its strategic oil stockpile from a disused mine at Ogies in eastern Mpumalanga province to a state storage facility at Saldanha Bay, near Cape Town.
Instead of physically moving the oil, the CEF sold oil from its Ogies stockpile and simultaneously bought oil on the open market and added it to the stockpile at Saldanha Bay.
The sales, beginning in 1989, initially outpaced purchases, which were accelerated in 1993 to restore the national stockpile to its original level.

The prices were adjusted to ensure that once the transfer was effected, the stockpile was still valued at the prices at which it was originally acquired and not at the prices that applied to the sale and purchase used to effect the transfer.

"The effect of this was to reduce the value of strategic stocks to their original cost plus transshipment cost as though the sale and repurchase of oil had not taken place," the auditor general said in the report.

"Even with the benefit of hindsight...in relation to the matters raised publicly by the minister thus far, we have not been able to identify any cases where we have failed to any material extent to do our duty to parliament, the taxpayer and the motorist."
